body: The sun is out over Jackson Square after Tuesday’s gray, thin and low and cold, and the Square has come out to meet it. Painters are hanging canvases on the iron fence. A woman at a card table sets down a deck of tarot cards and a thermos and pours the first cup of her shift. Mules in blankets stand in a row along Decatur with their carriages behind them and their breath going up, and in the middle of it all General Jackson sits his rearing bronze horse with his hat raised and a pigeon on it.
It took two buses and a walk. Kevin timed it: forty-one minutes, against thirty-eight on the schedule, and he would like it on the record that the three were the second bus’s.

Café du Monde sits on the corner under its green-and-white awning, packed to the curb with people in Saints jackets nursing the end of a week. Laney takes the one table with five chairs and orders for it before anybody is sitting, in a Dallas soprano that reaches the kitchen.

“Three orders of beignets, sir, that’s nine, I counted. Three café au laits. One hot chocolate for the fireman, because he is a child. And a black coffee for the Scandinavian, who is dead inside and proud of it.”
“Accurate,” Margot says.
“Yes, baby,” says the waiter, who writes none of it down, and goes.
Laney sits very straight. “He called me *baby*.”
“He called Kevin baby at the door,” Margot says.
“I felt seen,” says Kevin.
She has the Broussard’s Seafood notepaper unfolded beside her saucer, and Jack, reading it upside down, sees that the day has been divided into sections.

body.title: Laney’s list (Broussard’s Seafood notepaper, front)
body.text:
I. SUSTENANCE — Café du Monde (beignets x2, put down on purpose)
II. DEVOTION — the Cathedral (Kevin)
III. EDUCATION — that museum (Margot, do NOT let her start)
IV. THE RIVER (Theo, same)

body: The beignets come three to a plate under a drift of powdered sugar deep enough to lose a fork in, too hot to hold. Jack’s hot chocolate is thick enough to stand a spoon in. “For a child,” Laney says. “Obviously.” Margot takes one beignet off the nearest plate, wraps it in a napkin and puts it in her coat without explanation, and Kevin, who has given the warning at the bus stop, on the transfer and at the curb on Decatur, gives it a fourth time. “Do not exhale over the plate.”
Theo, in the camel coat, takes a pastry in both hands. “Picture it,” he says, and draws the breath for it. “A man, a coat, a pastry —”
He lets the breath go. The sugar rises in a single soft detonation past his face, hangs in the sun, and settles on him from collar to hem.
“Bless his heart,” Laney tells the table. “He never could hold it in.”
“I said it four times,” says Kevin. “Textbook acute sucrose exposure.”
Theo holds both arms out from his sides and lets the last of it settle. “I’ve been *floured*,” he says.
“You look like a Buick on Glenwood Avenue after the first snow,” Jack says.

“People love a Buick.” Theo accepts the loss of rank, and eats, and when the plate is clean he wraps the last beignet in a napkin and puts it in the pocket of the coat, where it can do no further harm.

The Cathedral stands across the Square behind its palms and its black iron, three spires and a clock face, and Kevin is already up and crossing to it at a walk that is just short of a run. At the foot of the steps he takes off his windbreaker and folds it over his arm, as he does at any church door in any weather.

Theo has dropped onto the nearest bench with the sugar still coming off his shoulders in the wind. “I’ll hold the coats,” he says. He hasn’t been offered one. Laney sits down beside him and hooks her arm through his. Kevin hands over the windbreaker, and Theo lays it across his knees with the zipped pocket up, the confiscated phone making a small flat lump in it, and looks at the palms.
“Costigan. Coat.”
“I’m good.” The RAZR and Lena’s tin ride in the Carhartt’s inside pocket, and it stays on.

Inside it is colder than the Square, a cold that comes up through his boots, and the sun comes in red and blue off the high windows and doesn’t warm a pew. Tourists go up the side aisles in sneakers with their cameras held to their chests. A docent at a pillar is whispering to six people about something over everyone’s head. The ceiling is painted a long way up. On an easel inside the door a card gives the day in somebody’s careful capitals: *Wednesday. Memorial of St. Scholastica, virgin.* Mémère’s finger on the calendar at seven this morning, and here the saint is again.

Kevin goes straight to the rack of votive candles at the side altar, puts a dollar through the slot of the box, lights a candle from another candle, and lights a second from the first. He says nothing about either. He walks up to a pew near the front and kneels with his forehead on his folded hands, and is still.

Jack takes a pew three rows back and kneels too. He says the Hail Mary because it is what he has. At the rack a boy about Rosie’s size is up on his toes with a taper nearly as long as he is, and his mother’s hands hover under his elbows the whole time he reaches. By *pray for us sinners* a baby behind Jack has started in on the ceiling, and the ceiling gives the complaint back to her twice.
Margot is waiting at the foot of the steps when they come out into the glare, with a paper napkin in her hand. She holds it out to Kevin without looking at him.
“Control group,” she says. “I set it aside at the table. I wanted to know if they hold.”
Kevin unwraps the beignet and bites it. “Do they?”
“They hold.” Margot turns to Jack. “Did you pray, or observe?”
“Hail Mary. Mostly I listened to a baby.”

“A recognized methodology.” She has already turned to the building next along, where a sign by the museum door has been waiting for her all morning. “The room where a continent changed hands,” she reads, off the building and the sign at once.

Kevin goes across to the bench for his windbreaker. Theo hands it up without a word, and Kevin runs a thumb down the zip of the inside pocket and puts it on. From where she sits, forty feet off, Laney’s voice crosses the walk with no effort at all. “On a *Wednesday*?”
Margot reads the sign again from the top, as if it might have changed, and does not answer.

From a shop door up Chartres a soprano saxophone is working through something slow and French over the scratch of a very old record. Jack stops in the sun to hear it out. Laney has Theo by the sleeve and is towing him toward the river, and Theo goes; Kevin and Margot are still at the museum door, one of them chewing. It is a minute and a half of tune and the needle at the end. He gives it all of that, and then goes after them across Decatur and up the long steps to the Moonwalk.

At the top the river is just there, all at once, wider than anything has a right to be: brown, and moving, and enormous, and cold from the far bank to the toes of his boots. The wind comes off it with an edge. A towboat shoves a raft of barges upstream against the current, a Lordstown parking lot of red steel making about the speed of a man walking, and the wake behind it folds over on itself for a quarter of a mile. Going the other way a ship rides so high its red bottom paint shows, with a man on the bridge wing eating an apple. Across the water Algiers is a low line of warehouses with the sun full on them.
Theo and Laney are along the rail with their backs to him and their heads together, Laney’s hands going the way they go when she is explaining something for the second time.
“— we don’t *touch* it, we don’t *say* it, we don’t even look *straight* at it —”
“At what?” Jack says.
Laney doesn’t turn. “My birthday,” she says, without a breath, and then she turns, full around, with a smile the width of the Mississippi. “It’s Sunday. Nobody is to do *anything*.”
“She means it,” Theo says, half a second behind. “Last year somebody hired a mariachi.”
“*Mama* hired a mariachi.”
“Nine men. One of them was a cousin.”
“Eight.”
“Eight,” Theo says. “One of them was a cousin.”
“I’ll tell the mariachi,” Jack says.
“Tell him gently.”

Kevin and Margot come up the steps behind Jack, Kevin with the last of the beignet and Margot with her hands in her coat. Laney rounds on them. “It is decided. We plan *nothing* for Sunday, because planning is how you jinx it.”
“Respectfully,” Kevin says, “that’s the first good plan either of you has had.”
Margot looks from Laney to Theo to the river. “Malinowski,” she says. “The Trobriand fishermen don’t waste a spell on the lagoon. It’s the open sea they chant over. I’m amending a note from Monday.”
“Margot, honey, *no*.” Laney hooks an elbow through Kevin’s and another through Margot’s and steers them off along the boardwalk toward a ship that has suddenly become urgent. Kevin looks back once.
That leaves Theo at the rail. The wind takes a streak of sugar off his shoulder and carries it out over the water, and he watches it go.
“Whatever this week is, Costigan —” He stops, and looks at the river.
“Never mind,” he says. “It’s a good week.”

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story. Tuesday morning I told him I think she’s the answer. He wanted a pamphlet, framed. Then he said nobody ever asked her to be that, and an answer is heavy for the person you hand it to. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no. At midnight, to the ceiling: don’t ever make me watch that again. Thursday he dressed me for the Palisades: his charcoal suit, pinned, and a half-Windsor — a commitment, like a coat. In the mirror he said I was good at it Wednesday, and that’s what he didn’t like. Friday: “You stayed.” She kept me there. “That’s love.” Saturday I tied his for the Pi Lam formal. He wanted the January call word for word. I gave it to him once. He asked if I know what I’m going to say tomorrow, if she asks. Monday: six days. Hollis was concerned; he told him I’d been detained by the Holy See. Monday night, two legal pads with Laney: a wedding seating chart, hypothetical. Tuesday he said Sigma Rho till two and left me the room. At a quarter to two he was in the lounge with Laney, Margot and Kevin: book club, *Dubliners*. He came in at twenty past two. Wednesday he pitched me New Orleans like a movie — the Saints, the money, and then, for the first time since I’ve known him, a favor. I need you there. I said no. That night I said yes, by text, from the stairs. Kevin drives the first shift. I drive West Texas. Thursday night he’d already paid my share. I made him take it back. He took a call from his mother at the edge of the lot: sandbags; they’re saying rain Friday night on the hill. At a quarter to five he hugged Skye a long time and said something only she heard. Friday night at a gas station in El Paso, by the ice machine, he and Laney said it was a mistake. The whole thing. I agreed with them. He went in and paid for the gas himself. Wednesday at Café du Monde he lost his whole camel coat to powdered sugar. He stayed outside the Cathedral and held the coats. On the Moonwalk he started to say something about this week, and didn’t. It’s a good week, he said.

choices.key: On the Moonwalk Theo started to say something about this week, and stopped, and said it’s a good week. It is, you said.
response: Theo nods at the river. Twice, short, and his mouth goes with it as though he is agreeing to terms. A towboat far downstream puts out one long note, and the wind takes the note and another streak of sugar off his shoulder together and carries both toward the Gulf.
“Say it again on Sunday,” Theo says.
From the top of the steps Laney’s voice comes down the levee in full soprano. “*Theodore! Costigan!* Margot has found a fortune-teller with a Ph.D., and they have started in on *methodology*!”

choices.text: “You’ve got sugar on your conscience, Vance.”
choices.key: On the Moonwalk Theo said it’s a good week. You told him he’s got sugar on his conscience. His conscience is cashmere, he said. It brushes off.
response: Theo looks down at his lapel, where the powder lies in the fold of the camel, and then at Jack.

“My conscience is cashmere,” he says. “It brushes off.” He brushes it, one slow stroke across his chest with the side of his hand, and a white streak goes out over the rail and down toward the water. “See?” Some of it doesn’t come off, and he leaves it. “Yours is wool, Costigan. Itches like sin and never wears out.”
Jack looks down at the Carhartt — canvas, a tin and a phone in the pocket, Interstate 10 in the seams — and has no argument.
“*Vance! Costigan!*” Laney, from the top of the steps. “Margot found a fortune-teller with a Ph.D., and she’s asking for her money back *before* the reading!”

choices.key: On the Moonwalk Theo started to say something about this week. You asked him what. Nothing, he said. Eat your beignet.
response: “Nothing.” Theo laughs, short, before the question is all the way out, and digs in the pocket of the camel coat and comes up with the napkin. The beignet has taken the shape of the pocket. “Eat your beignet.”

Jack takes it. It is cold and flat and still very good, and the sugar goes down the front of the Carhartt where Theo’s went down the camel. Theo watches the barges push upstream, one raft and then another behind it, slower than anything that gets anywhere. He offers nothing else, and Jack finishes the beignet.
“*Costigan!*” Laney, from the top of the steps, loud enough for Algiers. “The fortune-teller has a Ph.D., it’s from Tulane, and Margot is being *nice* to her!”
